concept.name: Information ratio
concept.definition: The ratio of active return (portfolio return minus benchmark return) to active risk (the tracking error, i.e. the standard deviation of the active return). It measures the consistency of a manager's value added per unit of benchmark-relative risk and is the natural analogue of the Sharpe ratio for benchmarked mandates.
concept.intuition: It grades the active bet itself: how much did deviating from the index earn, per unit of deviation risk taken?
concept.mechanics: Compute the active return series against the agreed benchmark, take its mean and its standard deviation (tracking error), and divide; annualize both components. Top-quartile managers historically achieve annualized IRs around 0.5 (Grinold and Kahn). Using regression alpha and residual risk instead yields the appraisal ratio.
concept.formula: IR = E[R_p - R_b] / sigma(R_p - R_b) = alpha / omega, where omega = sqrt(var(R_p - R_b)) is the tracking error.
concept.failure_modes: It is benchmark-dependent: the same manager posts different IRs against different indices, and gaming the benchmark (closet indexing with tilts) can flatter it. It uses arithmetic active returns and ignores leverage, so geometric-compounding effects can make a genuinely value-adding manager look negative.
concept.misconceptions: The IR numerator is simple active return, not Jensen's regression alpha — using regression alpha makes it the appraisal ratio, a different measure — and a high IR with tiny tracking error may reflect almost no real active management.
concept.example: A manager beating the benchmark by 2% per year with a 4% tracking error has an information ratio of 0.5, the level Grinold and Kahn associate with top-quartile performance.
